one_liner: HotSpot Java ring-of-nodes churn 1.49x faster than gcc -O3 C doing malloc/free per node; partly sin.
what_it_does: Two single-file programs (java_2_times_faster_than_c.c and Java2TimesFasterThanC.java, plus contributed C#, Go, Rust, Kotlin and JavaScript ports) build a doubly linked ring of 10,000 nodes, each carrying a 0-49 byte payload sized by fmod(sin(id * 100000.0) + 1, 1), then run 1,000,000 mutations that delete and insert up to 200 nodes each and print the node count and a checksum. The C version mallocs every node and its payload separately and frees both on delete; the Java version uses new and leaves dead nodes to the garbage collector. It is a benchmark, not a library.
how_it_is_fast: Two effects add up. Allocation: the JVM hands out memory from a heap it reserved at start-up (bump-pointer allocation, generational GC that never visits dead nodes), as issue #1 and #2 commenters note, while C pays two malloc and two free calls per node; issue #13's gprof profile puts malloc, _int_malloc, _int_free and free at about 13% of C run time and the inlined list work in main at 21.79%. Trigonometry: every node and mutation calls sin on arguments above glibc's 1.05e8 threshold, so glibc runs its slow __branred reduction (47.88% plus __sin_fma 17.32% in the same profile), while HotSpot's Intel LIBM sin intrinsic handles large arguments faster (1.26x in the repo's second benchmark).
when_to_use: Workloads that churn many small, short-lived, variable-size objects in a linked structure (caches, request pipelines) where the C alternative would call malloc and free per object: here the JVM's allocator and collector beat that pattern.
As a counter-example to 'garbage collection always costs throughput', citing the measured 1.49x rather than the title's 2x and noting the sin share.

As a starting harness for allocator experiments: the C file is about 100 lines, prints a checksum that every faithful port must match (node count 13537, checksum 470936697371), and is easy to rerun with a pool, an arena or another malloc.
when_not_to_use: When you control the C code: the author concedes better memory management in C can beat the Java version, and in issue #1 a one-slot node reuse cut an earlier version of the C program from 1m7s to 14s (no Java figure on that run).
Memory-constrained or embedded targets: JVM memory use was not measured, and the README itself lists a higher memory footprint as a reason not to use Java.
Short-lived processes where JVM start-up and JIT warm-up dominate (they are inside the 8.569 s here, but the run is long enough to hide them).
As evidence of a pure GC win: roughly a third of the measured gap is glibc's slow large-argument sin, and the sin-free xorshift64* variant in open PR #9 was never timed in text.
As a current result: one run from February 2021 on unstated gcc, glibc and JDK versions; the Rust rows predate the mimalloc change in PR #10 and were not rerun.

integration.dependencies: C: libc malloc and libm. Java: none at run time; the provided build uses the Gradle 6.8 wrapper with the Kotlin JVM plugin 1.4.21 and still lists the Bintray Kotlin EAP repository (dl.bintray.com).
integration.min_toolchain: JDK 15 (Gradle source and target level 15) and any C compiler with libm; the README results used gcc -O3 without -march=native.
integration.platforms: Measured only on x86-64 Linux (Intel Core i7-8550U, about 16 GB RAM); the sin share depends on glibc's x86-64 path and HotSpot's x86-64 sin intrinsic.
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (single-threaded benchmark programs; the JVM adds its own JIT and GC threads)

gotchas: Harness flaw: the 'pseudo-random' sizes come from sin on huge arguments, so most of the C time is libm, not memory management: issue #13's gprof profile shows __branred 47.88% plus __sin_fma 17.32% against about 13% for malloc and free, and a contributor's profile in PR #7 found 59% in almost_pseudo_random (clang build). With about 1e8 sin calls and the second benchmark's per-call times (64.4 ns C, 51.2 ns Java), sin explains roughly 1.3-1.7 s of the 4.2 s gap, and outside sin Java is still about 1.9-2.3x faster (derived estimate, assumes the per-call cost carries over).

Workload history: the January 2021 version (payloads up to 10,000 bytes; Java filled them with Arrays.fill, C with a raw byte loop that gcc did not turn into memset) showed C 1m21.495s vs Java 23.129s. After PR #7 switched C to memset, the contributor reported C about 5 s faster than Java, and commit 25d2bd8 then changed the workload (payloads up to 50 bytes, 10,000 initial nodes, 1e6 mutations of up to 200 nodes, per-byte fill loops in both); the current numbers come from that commit.

One shell 'time' run per language on a laptop CPU without frequency locking; the 'Clang' row (12.726 s) comes from build-clang.sh, which calls gcc, and the C build has no -march=native. Java's user plus sys time (8.818 s) is still well below C's 12.8 s, so extra JVM threads do not explain the gap.

The title says 2x and the README dialogue 'almost 2 times'; the measured ratio is 1.49x. The Go port ran different work (node count 13553, checksum 486105193130) because Go's sin returns different values.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The benchLANG HotSpot entry (Java 25, 2.9x over malloc/free C built with GCC 16.2.0) and LangArena Binarytrees::Obj (Java 27, 0.479 s vs 2.098 s for the best C/C++ build) show the same allocation effect with stated toolchains and no libm confound, so cite those first; use this one for its ring-mutation, variable-size-payload shape or for the documented history of how C fixes (memset, node reuse) erase the gap.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Core i7-8550U laptop, one shell 'time' run each: Java (HotSpot of the Java 15 era, default flags) 8.569 s vs the C version built with gcc -O3 -lm 12.800 s (12.726 s for a second gcc build labelled Clang), with identical node count 13537 and checksum 470936697371, about 1.49x (derived from page data). gcc, glibc and JDK versions are not stated, and a large share of the C time is glibc's large-argument sin rather than malloc and free.
status_note: Abandoned since February 2021 (README numbers from commit 25d2bd8 of 2021-02-04; open PR #9 with a sin-free xorshift64* generator was never merged or timed in text), GPL-3.0 and easy to rerun, but rerun it with a sin-free generator before citing it as a garbage-collection win.
